title: Annabelle Is in Salem: Inside the Haunted Warren Museum
excerpt: Annabelle and 1,000 Warren artifacts are on display at the Haunted Warren Museum in Salem this fall. What is inside, what tickets cost, and the no-phones rule.
content:
Annabelle has a new address, and it is the most on-brand one imaginable. The Haunted Warren Museum opened at 259 Essex Street in Salem, Massachusetts at the end of August, putting Ed and Lorraine Warren’s occult collection in front of the public for the first time since the couple’s Monroe, Connecticut basement museum closed in 2019. More than 1,000 artifacts are on display across 13 themed rooms, and the doll that launched a billion-dollar film franchise sits at the center of it.

It is a limited run. Tickets are on sale through Halloween, and the museum has said the Salem stay continues into December before the collection moves on.

How Annabelle Ended Up in Salem

The short version: comedian Matt Rife and YouTuber Elton Castee bought the Warrens’ Monroe home and museum in August 2025, weeks after NESPR investigator Dan Rivera died suddenly while touring the doll on the Devils on the Run tour. Rife has been careful to describe himself as Annabelle’s guardian rather than her owner. Per Conskipper, the artifacts remain the Warren family’s property, a point the Warrens’ son-in-law Tony Spera has made publicly, and are leased to the new operation.

The Connecticut house could not reopen to the public, which is the same zoning problem that shut the original museum. Castee told Conskipper the team looked for another Connecticut location and could not make one work under zoning and fire code. So they went to Salem, which is the one city in America that already budgets for a million Halloween tourists.

Even that took a fight. Tours of Salem reported in April that the project was off after the city council refused to grant operating hours past midnight in a residential neighborhood. By May, NBC Boston reported it was back on with approved hours to 11 p.m. on weeknights and midnight on weekends. “It’s been a process,” Castee told the station. “We’ve been working on this for eight, nine months in Salem alone.”

What Is Actually in the Building

The museum’s own exhibit list reads like a Conjuring Universe index: an Annabelle room, a Séance Parlor, a Witchcraft Forest, Possession & Exorcism, True Crime, a Haunted Playground and an Occult Barn. Named pieces include the Conjuring mirror, the Diamond Doll and a spirit photograph of Abraham Lincoln. CT Insider’s rundown adds the dinosaur toy from the Arne Cheyenne Johnson case that became The Devil Made Me Do It, a 17th-century witch’s door, Egyptian artifacts, and items connected to Jeffrey Dahmer, Ted Bundy, Charles Manson and Ed Gein.

Castee framed it to NBC Boston as something bigger than a relocation. “We’re not just bringing a few haunted items here,” he said. “We’re curating something really expansive.”

Worth knowing before you go: the original museum was a basement Ed Warren had blessed by a priest on a regular schedule, and the doll spent decades in a locked case with a warning sign on it. The Salem version is a 4,000-square-foot storefront that used to be a Blackcraft shop. Whether that changes anything is the kind of question the Warrens built a career on.

What It Costs, and the Rules

The standard ticket is the Flashlight Experience: a self-guided walk through all 13 rooms, up to an hour, lit by the flashlight they hand you. Pricing climbs with the calendar. September visits start at $49.99. October 1 through 28 is $66.60, which somebody clearly enjoyed typing. October 29 and 30 jump to $99.90, and Halloween night is $130, with a “free gift” included. A three-hour guided Paranormal Investigator Experience is listed as coming in November.

Two rules are absolute. Guests must be 12 or older, and anyone 12 to 17 needs a parent or guardian in the building with them the entire time. And no phones, cameras or recording devices of any kind are permitted inside. The museum’s exact words: “No exceptions.” The flashlight is the only thing you carry.

For the horror crowd, the timing is hard to beat. The Conjuring: Last Rites closed out the Warrens’ film saga last fall, and the real collection opening to the public a year later is the closest thing the franchise will get to a museum tour. Salem in October is already a pilgrimage. Now it has a demon doll.

Tickets and dates are at hauntedwarrenmuseum.com.
